The world

Digiday · October 7, 2026

Apple quietly widens its ad-tech blocklist, mid-Advertising Week

Apple reopened its war with ad tech a week before Advertising Week New York. iOS 27, released in mid-September, lets Safari's WebKit engine cut off companies that track people across the web without needing a software update: once a firm is added, Safari simply stops talking to it. Digiday tested more than 70 ad tech domains on October 7 and found five blocked so far: The Trade Desk, LiveRamp (being acquired by Publicis Groupe), ID5, Permutive and Experian's Audigent. Rivals Zeta's LiveIntent, Publicis-owned Lotame and Yahoo's ConnectID got through untouched. AdExchanger reports Apple has "hundreds of similar firms in its sights." The Trade Desk's own ad server was pulled from the blocklist in a test build of iOS, with a public rollout expected by the end of October.

Why it mattersOne unnamed ad executive described it to Digiday as "a slow death," not a crash. Apple does not need to ban an ID company outright, it just needs to make investors nervous. A platform quietly deciding who survives, one silent update at a time, is a bigger story than any single campaign launched at Advertising Week this year.
Digiday · October 6, 2026

Dhar Mann says he has $100 million pledged. Nobody has checked

Dhar Mann, Advertising Week New York's first-ever "chief creator officer," told the conference he already has pledges exceeding $100 million from CMOs for his Creator Challenge, to materialize within 12 months. He was careful to add that the number does not mean signed contracts this week: brand Q4 budgets lock in during Q1-Q2, they do not unlock on the spot. The pledges come from unnamed CMOs, and Digiday found no independent confirmation of any of them. Brad Hoos of The Outloud Group still praised Mann as a potential "connector" for a fragmented industry.

Why it mattersThe number is already circulating in trade coverage as fact, including in last issue of this brief. Worth remembering it is Mann's own claim, about his own event, with no third party behind it. That is not a scandal, it is just how a lot of advertising numbers get made.
Amazon Ads · October 7, 2026

Amazon's UK Upfront puts the whole portfolio on one stage

Amazon Ads held its annual UK Upfront on October 7 at Outernet in London, pitching advertisers on Prime Video, Prime Sports, Amazon MGM Studios, Twitch and Amazon Music as a single buy. Amazon says its ad business now reaches 8 of every 10 UK households, and that Prime Video alone delivers an average of more than 22 million monthly ad-supported viewers in the UK.

Why it mattersAmazon is selling reach the way a broadcaster used to, live sports and originals as the hook, ad tech as the upsell. It is the same move TikTok made a week earlier at Advertising Week New York (last issue): stop sending advertisers elsewhere, become the full stack yourself.
Digiday @ Advertising Week · October 7, 2026

Omnicom and Rembrand will slot brands into shows after they are already filmed

Omnicom Media is partnering with Rembrand, maker of the VISTA virtual-placement technology, to make AI-driven in-content advertising a standard media-plan line instead of a one-off sponsorship. Omnicom's RealID identity data is combined with streamer viewing data to find shows that over-index with a brand's target audience; Rembrand's system then maps those programs against specific scenes where a product can be inserted digitally, after filming has wrapped. A packaged-goods brand, for instance, could appear inside a cooking show without ever being on set.

Why it mattersThis only makes sense next to the Omnicom research below, 65% of US consumers actively avoid ads. If people leave the room for the ad break, the industry's answer is to stop having an ad break.

Campaigns & brand moves

Glossy / Digiday @ Advertising Week · October 8, 2026

Revlon reopens its own archive instead of chasing a trend

Revlon's "Be Unforgettable" campaign, fronted by Teyana Taylor and Megan Moroney since April, is a direct update of the brand's own campaign from the 1980s and '90s, the one that ran Cindy Crawford and Oprah Winfrey. Speaking at Advertising Week, Revlon North America president Dana Medema said the brand had "been quiet" and needed to reintroduce itself "not just to a next generation of consumers" but to its existing ones too. Agency DonerColle Partners built the relaunch around, in CEO Jessica Henrichs' words, "women of substance... more than just beautiful."

Why it mattersHeritage brands usually either ignore their own history or lean on it as pure nostalgia. Revlon is using its own archive as proof of a standard it is trying to hold itself to again, not just as a mood board.
Adweek / Digiday · October 6, 2026

An AI-native agency spoofs OpenAI to sell wet wipes

OK Future, a four-person agency founded by former MullenLowe US CEO Frank Cartagena and built around AI from its business plan to its website, made a new ad for founding client Goodwipes in four days. The spot spoofs OpenAI's Astra ad: the same shots of people quietly dictating to a screen, except the camera pulls back to reveal they are all sitting on the toilet. It is Goodwipes' running joke: the technique of wiping has not advanced since the 1800s no matter how advanced everything else gets.

Why it mattersFour people, four days, a real campaign for a real brand, timed to a cultural reference while it was still current. That production speed is the actual disruption, more than any single AI-generated frame.

What is working in content

Digiday @ Advertising Week · October 6, 2026

Omnicom's own data: 65% of US consumers avoid ads, on purpose

Omnicom Media's "From Tuned Out to Leaned In" study surveyed 1,136 US adults in August and ran behavioral eye-tracking research with eye square on another 1,200, testing four video formats: product placement, brand integration, augmented reality and standard pre-roll. The headline number: 65% of US consumers avoid advertising to some degree, 25% call themselves very or extremely active about it, and 41% pay for a subscription specifically to get away from ads. Chief intelligence officer Joanna O'Connell's framing: "Consumers are saying brands have permission, they just want it to be good."

Why it mattersThis is the research that justifies the Rembrand deal above. When avoidance is this high, the fix on the table is not a better 15-second spot, it is not looking like an ad at all.
Digiday · October 6, 2026

At Monks, AI agents now run for two days without anyone watching

S4 Capital's Monks has started letting AI agents work unsupervised for 36 to 48 hours at a stretch, mostly writing code for the agency's own software. Chief AI and revenue officer Wesley ter Haar says the coding agents run that long "without making mistakes," because code is precise and rule-bound. On multi-day projects, several agents split the work, test what they build against the original brief and review each other's output as they go, before a human looks at anything.

Why it mattersThe interesting shift is not that AI writes code, it is that nobody is in the loop for two days at a time. That is a production model, not a tool.

Social trends

TikTok · emerging, early October 2026

Patient Zero Wedding Day

  • Taylor Swift released "Patient Zero," her first single since marrying Travis Kelce, on September 25; its music video premiered at the VMAs with a staged "wedding photo" inside the song's fictional narrative.
  • TikTok creators are now cutting real wedding footage, proposals and "first look" clips to the track.
  • No platform view count has been published for the trend itself yet, only for the song's own rollout.
Why it mattersA reminder that a trend's real engine is often a single pop-culture release, not a platform algorithm. Watch the song's streaming numbers, not a TikTok dashboard, to see if this one has legs.
TikTok / Reels / Shorts · maturity unclear, flagged

Fan Transition, AI-assisted

  • Creators post one portrait and let an AI tool cycle through outfits, hairstyles and makeup looks, cut to look like each pass of a ceiling fan blade reveals a new one.
  • No platform has published adoption numbers and the format's actual start date is unclear, it shows up mostly on AI-tool marketing sites rather than creator or platform data.
Why it mattersFlagged specifically because it is a trend about not filming anything. If it is real at scale, it belongs next to Goodwipes and Monks above, as a third version of the same story: AI doing the production work a person used to do.
Pinterest · week of October 2, 2026

Pinterest's "Cozy Harvest Moon" week

  • Pinterest's own weekly trends report for October 2 lists real search growth: October Nail Ideas up 900%, Rainy Fall Outfits up 100%, Mini Pumpkin Painting Ideas up 100%, Caramel Apple Bar Ideas up 40%.
Why it mattersThese are Pinterest's own numbers, not an aggregator's estimate, which is rare enough in this brief to flag on its own. Nail ideas at +900% in one week is a real purchase-intent signal for beauty and DIY brands right now, not a maybe.

The historical bridge

Cincinnati, Ohio, 1881-82

99 and 44/100% pure: advertising's first precise, unverifiable number

In 1881 Harley Procter needed an angle for a new soap. He hired an outside chemist in New York, had him define "100% pure" as nothing but fatty acids and alkali, then sent in Ivory for testing. The consultant found 0.56% impurities, 99.44% pure by his own definition, measured against his own standard. Procter ran with "99 and 44/100% pure" starting in 1882, and it was still the headline of Ivory's advertising, decimal point included, in the 1919 ad shown here. Nobody outside Procter & Gamble ever checked the math.

Why it still holds. The specific decimal is what sold it: a round number would have read as marketing, a number with 44/100 in it reads as a measurement. That is exactly the trick behind "$100 million pledged by unnamed CMOs," or any other number in this week's news that nobody outside the room can check. A precise-sounding figure borrows credibility a vague one never gets, whether it is 1881 or 2026.
